statement: Wesley Thomas (Diné anthropologist/linguist), in published work on Navajo cultural constructions of gender and sexuality, describes a traditional FOUR-gender framework: asdzáán (women), hastiin (men), nádleehí (born male-bodied, functioning/living as feminine — a third gender), and a fourth gender, born female-bodied, functioning/living as masculine. Carolyn Epple, "Coming to Terms with Navajo Nádleehí: A Critique of Berdache, 'Gay,' 'Alternate Gender,' and 'Two-Spirit,'" American Ethnologist 25(2) (1998): 267-290, argues outside categorical frameworks — including the older anthropological term "berdache" and the pan-Indian "two-spirit" coinage (dated to a 1990 Winnipeg intertribal gathering, explicitly created to replace "berdache") — import premises (treating male/female as "mutually opposed, absolute values") that do not match how many Navajo people themselves construct nádleehí identity, which Epple frames as more situational/relational within Navajo cosmological logic than a fixed identity category comparable to Western LGBTQ categories. Nádleehí individuals are documented as historically holding valued spiritual/ceremonial roles specifically because of their dual masculine/feminine perspective.

sources.citation: Epple, Carolyn. "Coming to Terms with Navajo Nádleehí: A Critique of Berdache, 'Gay,' 'Alternate Gender,' and 'Two-Spirit.'" American Ethnologist 25(2), 1998: 267-290.
sources.author: Carolyn Epple

does_not_demonstrate: That "two-spirit" is a direct translation of nádleehí rather than a modern (1990-coined) pan-tribal English umbrella term some Diné people use in intertribal/public contexts alongside, not instead of, the older Navajo-specific category
